'''Corina Tarnita''' is a Romanian-American mathematician and theoretical biologist known for her work in [[Mathematical and theoretical biology|mathematical biology]] and [[Complex adaptive system|complex adaptive systems]]. She is currently the Frederick D. Petrie Professor of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Corina Tarnita {{!}} Ecology & Evolutionary Biology |url=https://eeb.princeton.edu/people/corina-tarnita |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=eeb.princeton.edu |language=en}}</ref> Her research examines how living organisms organize themselves into patterns at different scales. <ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Sokol |first=Joshua |date=2017-12-20 |title=A Mathematician Who Decodes the Patterns Stamped Out by Life |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-mathematician-who-decodes-the-patterns-stamped-out-by-life-20171220/ |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=Quanta Magazine}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Born in [[Craiova]], Romania, Tarnita showed an early aptitude for mathematics, encouraged by her mother, a professor of [[materials science]] and engineering.<ref name=":0" /> She won the Romanian National Mathematical Olympiad three times from 1999 to 2001.<ref name="Scientist-profile">{{Cite web |title=Corina Tarnita: The Ant Mathematician |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/corina-tarnita-the-ant-mathematician-41988 |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=The Scientist Magazine}}</ref> Tarnita moved to the United States to pursue higher education, obtaining her B.A. (2006), M.A. (2008), and Ph.D. (2009) in Mathematics from [[Harvard University]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Short Bio {{!}} Tarnita Lab @ Princeton |url=https://ctarnita.scholar.princeton.edu/biocv |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=ctarnita.scholar.princeton.edu}}</ref> She was a Junior Fellow in the [[Harvard Society of Fellows]] before joining the [[Princeton University]] faculty in 2013.<ref name=":1" />

== Research and career ==

Initially focused on high-dimensional mathematics, Tarnita was inspired by [[Martin Nowak]]'s work on [[evolutionary dynamics]] and shifted to studying [[mathematical biology]]. This change led her to complete her Ph.D. under Nowak's supervision, finishing in just three years.<ref name="Scientist-profile" />

Tarnita's 2010 paper, "The evolution of eusociality," co-authored with Martin A. Nowak and [[E. O. Wilson|Edward O. Wilson]], challenged the long-standing [[kin selection]] theory and proposed a new model for the evolution of [[eusociality]], sparking significant debate and reevaluation in the field of [[evolutionary biology]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nowak |first1=Martin A. |last2=Tarnita |first2=Corina E. |last3=Wilson |first3=Edward O. |date=August 2010 |title=The evolution of eusociality |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=466 |issue=7310 |pages=1057–1062 |doi=10.1038/nature09205 |pmid=20740005 |pmc=3279739 |bibcode=2010Natur.466.1057N |issn=1476-4687}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=harvardgazette |date=2010-08-25 |title=The ties that bind |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2010/08/the-ties-that-bind/ |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=Harvard Gazette}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Eusociality: A Question of Mathematics or Bad Science? {{!}} Writing Program |url=https://www.bu.edu/writingprogram/journal/past-issues/issue-6/hammond/ |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=www.bu.edu}}</ref> The response included a rebuttal published in ''[[Nature (magazine)|Nature]]'' from over a hundred researchers.<ref name=Abbot2011>{{cite journal |last1=Abbot |display-authors=etal |year=2011 |title=Inclusive fitness theory and eusociality |journal=Nature |volume=471 |issue=7339 |pages=E1–E4 |doi=10.1038/nature09831 |pmid=21430721 |pmc=3836173 |bibcode=2011Natur.471E...1A }}</ref>

Working with Princeton colleagues [[Robert M. Pringle|Robert Pringle]] and Juan Bonachela, Tarnita developed new theories about the formation of large, [[patterns in nature|regular vegetation patterns]], such as [[Fairy circle (arid grass formation)|fairy circles]] in the [[Namib Desert]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Page |first=Thomas |date=2017-01-31 |title=Fairy circles: Has one of nature's great mysteries been solved? |url=https://www.cnn.com/travel/article/namibia-fairy-circles-mystery-new-theory/index.html |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=CNN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tarnita |first1=Corina E. |last2=Bonachela |first2=Juan A. |last3=Sheffer |first3=Efrat |last4=Guyton |first4=Jennifer A. |last5=Coverdale |first5=Tyler C. |last6=Long |first6=Ryan A. |last7=Pringle |first7=Robert M. |date=January 2017 |title=A theoretical foundation for multi-scale regular vegetation patterns |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20801 |journal=Nature |volume=541 |issue=7637 |pages=398–401 |doi=10.1038/nature20801 |pmid=28102267 |bibcode=2017Natur.541..398T |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Tarnita's research on "loner" behavior in [[slime mold]]s revealed that this seemingly non-cooperative trait is actually an [[evolutionarily stable strategy]], challenging previous assumptions about social behavior in [[microorganism]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tarnita |first1=Corina E. |last2=Washburne |first2=Alex |last3=Martinez-Garcia |first3=Ricardo |last4=Sgro |first4=Allyson E. |last5=Levin |first5=Simon A. |date=2015-03-03 |title=Fitness tradeoffs between spores and nonaggregating cells can explain the coexistence of diverse genotypes in cellular slime molds |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=112 |issue=9 |pages=2776–2781 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1424242112 |doi-access=free |pmc=4352809 |pmid=25605926|bibcode=2015PNAS..112.2776T }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=University |first=Princeton |title=Evolution selects for 'loners' that hang back from collective behavior—at least in slime molds |url=https://phys.org/news/2020-03-evolution-loners-behaviorat-slime-molds.html |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=phys.org}}</ref>

In 2024, Tarnita was named a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Corina Tarnita – John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation… |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/corina-tarnita/ |access-date=2025-01-19 |language=en}}</ref>

===Relationship with Jeffrey Epstein===
Tarnita met convicted sex offender [[Jeffrey Epstein]] while she was a graduate student working under Nowak at Harvard in 2008. She remained in contact with Epstein through 2012, including emails that refer to his 2008 conviction.<ref name="whitford">{{cite news |last1=Whitford |first1=Emma |title=Even More Higher Ed Names in the Epstein Files |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/faculty-issues/2026/02/05/even-more-higher-ed-names-epstein-files |access-date=20 April 2026 |work=Inside Higher Ed |date=5 February 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In 2009, she helped Epstein anonymously wire transfer $10,000 and $5,000 respectively to two Romanian women for scholarships.<ref>{{cite news |last1=O'Neill |first1=Bridget |last2=Grippo |first2=Luke |title=Princeton professor maintained sustained communication with Epstein from 2008 to 2012 |url=https://www.dailyprincetonian.com/article/2026/02/princeton-news-broadfocus-epstein-corina-tarnita-wire-transfer-trip-island |work=[[Daily Princetonian]] |date=February 3, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Garisto |first1=Dan |title=Epstein files reveal deeper ties to scientists than previously known |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00388-0 |work=[[Nature (journal)]] |date=February 6, 2026 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/OCTan |archive-date=February 9, 2026|quote="A spokesperson for Princeton confirmed Tarnita’s account by showing Nature e-mails from 2008 between Tarnita and a Romanian academic, which corroborate that the wire transfers were for scholarships."}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Martin |first1=Emmy |title=Here's What the Latest Epstein Files Say About His Ties to Higher Ed |url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/heres-what-the-latest-epstein-files-say-about-his-ties-to-higher-ed |work=[[Chronicle of Higher Education]] |date=February 2, 2026}}</ref>
